results.note: Checked the supplied Slavova article text, Methodologic Considerations, third paragraph (saved-text line 73), and reference 45 (Hargrove et al., 2018). The review explicitly attributes the rise from 2.9% to 17% to routine gabapentin testing beginning in July 2014 and gives the warning about gradual procedural changes. This confirms the review's report, not an independently read Hargrove study. These are proportions with detected gabapentin among people who died of drug overdose, not evidence that gabapentin caused those deaths or that total overdose mortality rose by that amount. The saved article contains no underlying case counts from which those two percentages can be recomputed.

Checked original PDF pages 1-4 (printed 189-192), own 150-dpi body pages and 300-dpi Table 1 on PDF page 2. The false-negative definition is in Methods/Materials paragraph 5 on printed 190, with a typographical omission in the phrase "very low or suspicion"; Results and Table 1 independently identify the 115 cases with no suspicion before autopsy but a drug-toxicity final cause after toxicology. The Discussion first paragraph continues across both columns on printed 191 and contains the stated majority, 11%-13%, and 60-of-629/three-pathologist/75%-80% summaries. The other studies were not independently read. Own Table 1 reconstruction gives 115/237=48.5232% (Wilson 95% 42.2348%-54.8587%), 265/2719=9.7462%, sensitivity 95.5236%, specificity 31.5245%. The opening Results paragraph swaps preliminary and final margins; the table and following case descriptions support the frozen counts. The study does not directly compare an independently assigned external-examination-plus-toxicology diagnosis against autopsy. Its 265 false positives include negative toxicology, so any autopsy-only contribution remains unquantified.

Checked original PDF page 2 (printed 153) at 150 dpi and reference 15 on PDF page 7 (printed 158) at 150 dpi. Question 1 paragraph 1 cites Dye et al., 2019 for reduced accuracy even with suggestive scene findings, with no numeric accuracy figure supplied there. Paragraph 5 permits deferring autopsy in the selected delayed-death subset and calls for review from hospital admission to death and seeking admission blood or urine. Reference 15 identifies the drug-toxicity study, but its full text was not supplied or independently read. The surrounding statement should retain "may be deferred in selected delayed deaths"; this is permission for a subset, not a blanket rule that every delayed overdose death receives records review instead of autopsy. The panel's 20%-30% figure elsewhere in Question 1 has a different citation set (6,8-13), not Dye.

Checked original PDF pages 5-6 (printed 546-547), own 150-dpi body images, and Table 1 on PDF page 3 (printed 544) at 300 dpi. Discussion paragraph 1 begins at printed 546 bottom right and continues at printed 547 top left, as proposed. Independently summing Table 1 gives access (78+1012)/1320=82.5758%, none 148/1320=11.2121%, and not-needed 82/1320=6.2121%. The article reports about 300 offices with five or fewer deaths but does not provide their underlying observations. The rural/frontier explanation is specifically offered for offices saying toxicology was not needed; possible processing by an autopsy provider or state medical examiner is offered for offices reporting no access. These are self-reported office capabilities, with imputation and response-interpretation concerns discussed on printed 548, not a measured share of deaths receiving no testing.

All of the intent percentages and the policy explanation occur in the fourth paragraph of the named subsection (saved-text line 75). The first paragraph (line 69) concerns completeness of drug specification and gives the 92%,71%,73%,62% system comparison, not the intent figures in this extraction. The extraction itself is supported as a second-hand review summary; the corrected locator removes the irrelevant first paragraph. Neither Warner et al. nor the CDC WONDER data were independently read, and no system-type inference for these states was added.
results.corrected_extracted: As the review reports: Warner et al. (2013) found 85% of poisoning deaths in Maryland and over 40% in Utah classed as undetermined intent against 8% nationally; as of 2016 the share of drug poisoning deaths with undetermined intent still ranged from 1% (Connecticut, Massachusetts) to 68% (Maryland), and the authors suggest that medical examiner and coroner office policies not aligned with professional recommendations may influence this variation; the review does not name the states' system types here.

Checked the supplied Gutkind saved article text, methods on review/extraction and absence of study risk-of-bias assessment, Results 2.1/Table 1 Warner row (saved-text lines 103-108), the table's definitions at line 111, and reference 17. The row explicitly lists national NVSS multiple-cause-of-death data for 2008-2010 and distinguishes undetermined manner varying by state but not system from drug specification varying by both. Table 1 and the Methods equation are supported. I transcribed the seven retained states from the 300-dpi original Table 1 and inspected Figure 1/Table 4 on PDF page 5 at 300 dpi, plus body pages 3-4 at 150 dpi. The figure is a descriptive comparison of trajectories and relative levels; it does not estimate or test state-specific reform effects. Massachusetts is already below Pennsylvania before the switch, and West Virginia is briefly above Indiana just after it. Results paragraph 1 attributes the large common drops in the first four pairs to adoption of ICD-9; a similar drop predates the Massachusetts switch. The correction makes these limits explicit so the surrounding statement does not present different plotted levels as demonstrated causal effect heterogeneity. No state-specific estimates or repeated-state error adjustment is stated in the supplied paper. Normal 95% intervals from the rounded Table 4 estimates/SEs recompute to -0.0984 to 0.0584, -0.1280 to 0.0680, and -0.1376 to 0.0976; these are conditional editorial intervals, and the paper does not establish how a repeated-state adjustment would change them.
results.corrected_extracted: Before the switch, two of the seven analysed states used justices of the peace (West Virginia, Arizona), two used coroners (New Mexico, New Jersey), and one each used a physician coroner (Massachusetts), a locally appointed physician (New Hampshire) and a magistrate coroner (Alaska) (Table 1; Delaware and Florida were excluded from analysis). The paper specifies one difference-in-differences equation for the pooled state-year observations, fitted over three time windows, and states no adjustment for repeated observations within a state. Figure 1 shows differing descriptive trajectories and relative levels: after the switch New Jersey remains above New York; New Mexico and, in most later post-switch years, West Virginia are below Idaho and Indiana; Massachusetts is below Pennsylvania both before and after its switch; and Arizona and Nevada show broadly similar post-switch movements. The authors attribute the sharp common drops in the first four pairs to the introduction of ICD-9 coding, with a comparable drop occurring before the Massachusetts switch. No state-specific reform-effect estimates or formal test of effect heterogeneity is reported, so these plots alone do not show that reform had different causal effects in different states.

results.note: Own 150-dpi Results page 5 and 300-dpi Table 1 page 6 confirm the printed values and reversed mean order. Independently transcribed cell n/means/SDs produce pooled within-cell SD=4.9271, equal-marginal age F≈4.6264, age-by-drug F≈5.4295 and age-within-ecstasy F≈10.0719. Thus the proposed approximate calculations are reproducible. The correction removes a reference to an unread card and makes the inference limit explicit: Table 1 header counts sum to 1248, whereas the reported residual df=1230 imply N=1238 under the stated eight-cell model. Rounded summaries and those unmatched counts do not identify the exact analysis or prove that F=4.8 was the interaction. Surrounding magnitude wording should say that the F is more consistent with an interaction than the simple ecstasy-age comparison in an approximate reconstruction, rather than stating that it "recomputes as" a known test. The descriptive older-younger mean direction is well supported; an exact corrected test remains unverified without analytic data/output.
results.corrected_extracted: The Results report higher harm-reduction support after the older rather than the younger person's story (F(1,1230)=4.5, p=.035), but print the means in the order 22.98 (SD 5.09) versus 23.57 (SD 4.78). They report no significant main effect of gender (printed F=.0, p=.802) or drug (printed F=.0, p=.922). A profile-plot discussion of the age-by-drug interaction describes higher support after the older rather than younger person in the ecstasy story, while printing F(1,1230)=4.8, p=.029 and means 22.7 (SD 5.4) versus 23.89 (SD 4.67). Table 1 stigma condition means range from 38.6 for Jane/younger/ecstasy to 50.1 for John/older/heroin. Independent editorial calculations using the rounded Table 1 cell summaries and header group sizes give harm-reduction means of 23.575 for older versus 22.974 for younger stories, 23.899 versus 22.652 within ecstasy stories, and 23.251 versus 23.299 within heroin stories. These support the authors' narrative direction and indicate that the two printed older-younger mean pairs are reversed. With a pooled within-cell SD of 4.927, approximate equal-marginal contrasts give F=4.63 for age, F=5.43 for age-by-drug and F=10.07 for age within ecstasy. The printed F=4.8 is therefore more consistent with the interaction than with the within-ecstasy age comparison in this reconstruction, but its exact identity cannot be established: the cell values are rounded, Table 1 header counts sum to 1248, and the reported residual degrees of freedom imply 1238 observations under the stated full eight-cell model. These F values are diagnostic editorial approximations, not an exact reanalysis. The older-younger contrast also changes the depicted person's drug-use history.
